steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper arguing that a linear attention model is a good simplified abstraction for studying why Transformer optimization is hard. Explain the difficulty of training Transformers, what the literature has found about their loss landscape, why we need a simpler model, and our main contributions.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Transformer architectures (from here on just called Transformers) have shown impressive performance in many applications. However, it is well known that training Transformers is difficult and laborious; see for example the observations in prior work as well as scaling laws. In particular, to train Transformers you need carefully designed optimizers and also various heuristics. For example, as Figure 1 shows, stochastic gradient descent (SGD), which is the workhorse for most deep learning optimization problems, does not train Transformers effectively. This is different from how SGD succeeds when it is used to train convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on vision tasks.

Several recent papers give a number of different explanations for why Transformer optimization is so difficult. The literature generally agrees that the loss landscape of Transformers has a number of distinctive features that are significantly different from the assumptions of standard optimization theory. Most notably, various experiments have verified empirically that stochastic gradient noise is heavy-tailed and non-Gaussian and that the loss landscape is significantly ill-conditioned. Standard assumptions cannot deal with or explain these observations, and because of this Transformer optimization has become more of an art than a science.

- Obstacle: full Transformers extremely complicated to model
  - gradient norm / smoothness measurable, inner layers hard to parse
  - why landscape features? why Adam > SGD?
- Abstraction: simple but captures essence
  - main message: linear attention model (no nonlinear activations, no feedforward networks)
  - low-dimensional linear regression -> all distinctive features -> testbed
- Main contributions
  - shallow linear Transformer on random linear regression, reproduces all features
  - vary data distribution, number of layers: more heavy-tailed data / more layers -> more pronounced
- Outlook: theory + optimization methods, future work; next survey previous works

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Transformer architectures (from here on just called Transformers) have shown impressive performance in many applications. However, it is well known that training Transformers is difficult and laborious; see for example the observations in prior work as well as scaling laws. In particular, to train Transformers you need carefully designed optimizers and also various heuristics. For example, as Figure 1 shows, stochastic gradient descent (SGD), which is the workhorse for most deep learning optimization problems, does not train Transformers effectively. This is different from how SGD succeeds when it is used to train convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on vision tasks.

Several recent papers give a number of different explanations for why Transformer optimization is so difficult. The literature generally agrees that the loss landscape of Transformers has a number of distinctive features that are significantly different from the assumptions of standard optimization theory. Most notably, various experiments have verified empirically that stochastic gradient noise is heavy-tailed and non-Gaussian and that the loss landscape is significantly ill-conditioned. Standard assumptions cannot deal with or explain these observations, and because of this Transformer optimization has become more of an art than a science.

A big obstacle to understanding Transformer optimization is that full Transformers are extremely complicated to model. You can probe the properties of a Transformer by measuring things like gradient norm or smoothness, but it is much harder to parse how the inner layers work, and to answer questions like why the loss landscape has such features, or how algorithms like Adam do better than SGD in Transformer training.

So to make progress in understanding Transformer optimization we need an appropriate mathematical abstraction, one that is as simple as possible but can still capture the essence of Transformer optimization. The main message of this paper is that the distinctive features of Transformer training also show up in a much simpler setting: the linear attention model, without nonlinear activations and feedforward networks, is exactly the abstraction we are looking for. We verify that training this model on a low-dimensional linear regression task shows all the distinctive features that have been seen on the full Transformer, which suggests that our surprisingly simple model can be a testbed for a rigorous understanding of Transformer optimization.

Main contributions. Our main contributions are:

- We propose training a shallow linear Transformer model on random linear regression as a model for understanding Transformer optimization. We verify that this model reproduces all of the optimization features and phenomena previously reported for full Transformers.

- Because our model is simple, we can look deeper into how these features come about, by changing the settings (e.g., data distribution, the number of layers). The results show that the unique features from previous work become more pronounced in our linear Transformer setting when the data distribution is more heavy-tailed, or when the number of layers increases.

We expect that a simple abstraction like this is very valuable for theoretical research and also for developing optimization methods for Transformers. But these directions are out of scope for this work and are left for future work. First, as a preliminary, we survey the previous works that try to characterize and understand the Transformer optimization landscape.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Transformer architectures [1] (henceforth referred to as Transformers) have shown impressive performance in various applications [2,3]. However, training Transformers is notoriously difficult and laborious; see, e.g., the observations given by [4] as well as scaling laws [5]. In particular, training Transformers requires carefully designed optimizers as well as various heuristics. For instance, as illustrated in Figure 1, stochastic gradient descent (SGD), the workhorse of most deep learning optimization problems, fails to train Transformers effectively. This is in contrast to the success of SGD in training convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on vision tasks.

Several recent papers propose different explanations of why Transformer optimization is so difficult. There is a general consensus in the literature that the loss landscape of Transformers has a number of distinctive features that differ significantly from the assumptions of standard optimization theory. Most notably, various experiments have empirically verified that stochastic gradient noise is heavy-tailed and non-Gaussian [6,7] and that the loss landscape is significantly ill-conditioned [8,9,10]. Standard assumptions are incapable of explaining these observations, and as a result, Transformer optimization has become more of an art than a science.

A major obstacle in understanding Transformer optimization is that full-fledged Transformers are extremely complicated to model. One can probe a Transformer's properties by measuring quantities such as gradient norm or smoothness, but it is much harder to parse the workings of the inner layers and to satisfactorily answer questions such as: why does the loss landscape have such features, or how do algorithms like Adam outperform SGD in Transformer training?

Therefore, progress in understanding Transformer optimization requires an appropriate mathematical abstraction, one that is as simple as possible while still capturing the essence of Transformer optimization. The main message of this paper is that the distinctive features of Transformer training also arise in a far simpler setting: the linear attention model, without nonlinear activations and feedforward networks, is precisely the sought abstraction. We verify that training this model on a low-dimensional linear regression task displays all the distinctive features observed on the full Transformer, suggesting that our surprisingly simple model can serve as a testbed for a rigorous understanding of Transformer optimization.

Main contributions. Our main contributions are as follows:

- We propose the problem of training a shallow linear Transformer model on random linear regression as a model for understanding Transformer optimization, and verify that this model reproduces all the optimization features and phenomena previously reported for full Transformers.

- We leverage the simplicity of our model to look deeper into how these features arise by changing the settings (e.g., data distribution, the number of layers). Our results reveal that the unique features from previous work become more pronounced in our linear Transformer setting when the data distribution is more heavy-tailed or the number of layers increases.

We expect such a simple abstraction to be of great value not only for theoretical research but also for the development of optimization methods for Transformers. These directions, however, are out of scope of this work and left for future work. As a preliminary, we first survey previous works that seek to characterize and understand the Transformer optimization landscape.
